fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: 47 Tests, One Headline, Zero Replication
fieldNotes.source: Anonymous senior analyst at Paisa Vault, a Pune-based consumer-fintech startup
fieldNotes.story:
On March 11, 2025, the growth-analytics team at Paisa Vault published a celebrated internal note titled *"Why Tier-2 Cities Convert 1.8x Better Than Tier-1."* It went up on the company wiki, got pinned in #all-hands, and was quoted by the CEO in the next investor update. The methodology section, in tiny font on page 4, read: *"Logistic regression with city-tier as predictor; p = 0.043."*

What the note did not mention: the same analyst had run **47 hypothesis tests** that week against the same Q4 dataset. Tier, age bucket, gender, device type, referral source, time-of-day, day-of-week, NPS bucket, lifetime-value decile, and 38 others. **One** of them, by sheer luck of the multiple-comparisons fairy, came in at p < 0.05. That one became *"the finding."* The other 46 went into the recycle bin.

In April, the product team rolled out a Tier-2 acquisition push based on the note. Six weeks of paid marketing, ₹38 lakh of spend. **Conversion lift: -0.4 percent.** Replication on Q1 data: p = 0.71. The growth lead, in the post-mortem on May 2, said the line that everyone now quotes back: *"We didn't have a finding. We had a coincidence with a confidence interval."*

The analyst still works there. The note is still on the wiki, with a banner now: *"RETRACTED — see post-mortem."*
fieldNotes.takeaway: If you torture a dataset long enough, it will confess to anything. State your hypothesis before you touch the data, or don't dignify what comes out as a finding.

bossBattle.title: Boss Battle: Is Churn Really Up?
bossBattle.setup:
It's **Day 4** of Aditi's first week at Vyapaar Money, a Mumbai consumer-credit fintech. She has a fresh laptop, a still-sticky onboarding mug, and Slack DM from her boss at 9:47am: *"Quick one. The leadership offsite is Friday. Is churn really up this quarter? Need a one-liner I can put on a slide. Thanks!"*

Aditi opens the data warehouse. She has access to 14 tables, three years of history, and exactly **48 hours**. She pings you, her unofficial mentor.

coach.name: Staff-DS Sandeep
coach.role: Staff data scientist, six startups in, allergic to dashboards without denominators

stages.prompt: Aditi types: *"I'll just pull churn rate by month for Q3 and Q2, eyeball it, send the number."* What do you tell her **first**?

options.label: "Sounds good, ship it. Sandeep is busy."
options.explain: Sandeep watches Aditi's slide land in Friday's deck with the words *churn is up 14 percent.* Three weeks later the cohort team finds it was a denominator change — the product redefined 'active user' in August. Aditi's slide is now in a board memo. Sandeep emails her, gently.

options.label: "Before you query: write down what 'churn is up' would actually have to look like in the data to be true. Then go look."
options.explain: **Yes.** Hypothesis first, data second. Aditi writes: *churn is up = the cohort-adjusted 90-day retention curve in Q3 sits below the same curve in Q2 by more than the noise of the last 6 quarters.* Now she knows what query to write and what answer would actually settle it.

options.label: "Run 20 cuts of the data — by city, age, plan, device — and find the most dramatic chart."
options.explain: This is the Paisa Vault playbook from the field notes. Run enough cuts and one will look dramatic by chance alone. Aditi will ship a coincidence and call it a finding. Hard pass.

options.label: "Just ask the boss what answer he wants and back into it."
options.explain: Sandeep would like a word. This is how analysts become rubber stamps and then get blamed in retros for findings that weren't theirs to begin with.

stages.prompt: Aditi writes the hypothesis. She pulls Q2 and Q3 churn. Q2: 4.1 percent. Q3: 4.6 percent. She's about to Slack: *"churn up 12 percent QoQ."* What do you say?

options.label: "Looks decisive. Send it."
options.explain: 12 percent relative jump on a base of 4 percent is well inside the noise band of a quarterly metric on a fintech with seasonality. She's about to call a wave a tide.

options.label: "What's the quarter-on-quarter noise floor for the last 8 quarters? If Q1 to Q2 also moved 12 percent in random directions, this isn't a signal."
options.explain: **Exactly.** Aditi pulls the historical series and finds Q-on-Q swings of -9, +14, -6, +11, -3, +8, -7 percent over the last two years. Q3's +12 is unremarkable. The 'finding' dissolves on contact with context.

options.label: "Run a t-test on daily churn rates across the two quarters, report the p-value."
options.explain: A t-test on daily churn rates with n in the thousands will return p < 0.001 on tiny effect sizes that don't matter. She'll get statistical significance and zero practical significance. Wrong tool for the question.

options.label: "Segment by acquisition cohort first — a mix shift in new users can fake a churn spike."
options.explain: **Smart.** If Vyapaar acquired a flood of low-quality referral users in late Q2, Q3 churn looks worse without the underlying retention curve changing at all. Cohort-adjust before you call it a trend.

stages.prompt: Aditi cohort-adjusts. The Q3 curve is 0.3 points below Q2 — well inside historical noise. Boss wants a one-liner. **What does she write?**

options.label: "Churn is up 12 percent QoQ." (one number, no caveats)
options.explain: Confidently wrong. The number is real but the framing is misleading. Cohort-adjusted, there's no signal. This sentence will outlive the truth in every deck for the next six quarters.

options.label: "Headline churn ticked up from 4.1 to 4.6 percent QoQ, but cohort-adjusted retention is flat — within historical noise. No real change yet."
options.explain: **Ship this.** Specific numbers, the apparent move, the corrected interpretation, and a calibrated conclusion. Boss can put this on a slide and defend it from any VP who pulls on the thread.

options.label: "Churn analysis is complicated. Need more time."
options.explain: The work is done. This is a confidence problem masquerading as a thoroughness problem. Boss reads this as 'Aditi can't summarize.'

options.label: "Cohort-adjusted retention is flat. The 12 percent headline move is a mix-shift artifact from the June referral campaign."
options.explain: **Even better — names the cause.** If Aditi can point to the mechanism (June referral cohort dragging down headline numbers without affecting underlying retention), the boss now has a *story*, not just a number. That's a senior-analyst move.

outcomes.perfect: You walked Aditi from 'pull a number' to 'state a hypothesis, check the noise floor, cohort-adjust, write a defensible one-liner' in under two days. Sandeep buys you a vada pav. This is what a data mental model looks like in practice.
outcomes.good: Decent instincts on most of it. The hypothesis-first reflex is the muscle worth building — re-read the lesson on framing before the next ad-hoc request, because the next one is already in your DMs.
outcomes.learn: Aditi shipped a slide that didn't survive contact with a curious VP. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **stating the hypothesis before querying** and **noise floors before headlines**. The Paisa Vault retraction is a preview, not a punchline.
